newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban say roll back "evil forces".
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban say roll back "evil forces".

text.p: Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban movement said on Thursday it had rolled back the forces of former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood from positions close to the capital Kabul and was advancing north.

Hopes for a peaceful solution to the conflict were raised on Wednesday when the Taleban opened talks with powerful northern chief Abdul Rashid Dostum, the first known high-level contact between the two sides.

Taleban-held Radio Afghanistan said its forces had retaken the village of Qarabagh, 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul, and a crossroads leading to Bagram airbase, the scene of heavy fighting since Masood's forces swept south late last week.

"In continuation of its mopping up operations, the Islamic army cleared Qarabagh and Chaikal-Robat up to the Bagram intersection completely of the forces of evil and corruption," Taleban-controlled Radio Afghanistan said.
"The Islamic army is dominant in the area and is advancing," it said.

Reports from the frontline confirm that after a lightning strike across the plains south of their Hindu Kush stronghold, Masood's forces have run up against stiff resistance less than an hour's drive north of Kabul.

There was no sign of reinforcements from northern leader Abdul Rashid Dostum, Reuters correspondent Kurt Schork reported, throwing into question whether an agreement signed earlier this week between the two former rivals would bear fruit.

The Taleban, Islamic purists from southern Afghanistan who swept to power in a dramatic offensive last month, appear to have rallied after a similarly dramatic retreat across the plains north of Kabul earlier this week.
Denying they were on the defensive, the turbanned fighters have reinforced defences around the capital and shipped in hundreds of volunteers from outer regions.
Fighting now appears to be confined to a shifting frontline around the town of Charikar and Bagram, a strategic airbase that has so far remained in Taleban hands, travellers said.
At least 800 people have been wounded in the country's latest bout of fighting, the International Committee of the Red Cross reported from Geneva on Wednesday.

Kabul itself remained quiet but tense, as relief that an expected assault on the city had not materialised was tempered with foreboding about fighting beyond the hills overshadowing the northern fringe of the capital.
"We know that there is fighting going on out there, and we are used to it. But we are just praying that God willing it does not return to Kabul," said one market vendor.

Wednesday's meeting between Dostum and the Taleban, apparently brokered by Pakistan and held in territory under Dostum's control, was due to continue on Thursday on the proposed formation of a commission to decide the country's political future.
